SyncGuard AI: Final Project Report

Pricing & Inventory Sync Anomaly Detector

Team 14 · generated November 21, 2026

1. Executive summary

SyncGuard AI learns what normal price and inventory syncing looks like using an unsupervised autoencoder and flags syncs that deviate, so operations teams can fix integration problems before customers see them. It is delivered as a data pipeline, a model, a FastAPI detection service and an interactive dashboard.

90.4%Held-out precision
93.0%Held-out recall
91.7%Held-out F1
0.996ROC-AUC
0.905PR-AUC

2. Problem

Retailers selling on several channels depend on automated syncing of prices, stock and availability. Failures create stale prices, wrong stock and overselling. Fixed-threshold monitoring only catches what someone thought to configure, and misses combined or subtle problems. An autoencoder learns normal behavior from data and flags anything it cannot reproduce.

3. Data pipeline

65,059 raw rows were cleaned to 64,800 (259 duplicates removed, 902 gaps filled, 129 impossible values fixed). Full details are in the Dataset Preparation Report.

4. Feature engineering

Feature How it is computed Why it matters
price_diff_pct (channel price / master price) / channel's normal ratio − 1 Catches wrong or stale prices and decimal slips
stock_diff_pct (channel stock − fair share of master stock) / fair share Catches inventory that drifted from the master
sync_delay_log log(1 + minutes since last sync) Catches late or stopped integrations (log tames the long tail)
stock_cover_hours log(1 + channel stock / units sold per hour) Catches oversell risk: stock running out faster than expected
price_change_pct channel price % change minus master price % change since the previous record (capped) Catches sudden price jumps the master did not make
stock_change_pct channel stock % change minus master stock % change since the previous record (capped) Catches sudden stock jumps the master did not make (shared restocks cancel out)
sync_attempts_log log(1 + number of attempts the sync needed) Catches integrations that keep retrying
update_gap_log log(1 + minutes since the previous update of the same product and channel) Catches irregular update intervals and missing updates
sync_status_code 0 = success, 1 = retry, 2 = failed (categorical, encoded as a number) Catches syncs the integration itself reported as failing

5. Autoencoder model

A scikit-learn MLPRegressor with architecture 9 → 4 → 9 (tanh) is trained to reproduce its input. Training is label-free and two-pass: a first model scores the training rows, the most unusual 4% (1,815 rows) are dropped as probable errors, and the model is retrained on the cleaned set. Training used 45,360 rows and 37 iterations.

Architecture experiments

architecture normal_mse precision recall f1 seconds iterations
9 → 3 → 9 0.305 0.606 0.997 0.754 4.900 60
9 → 4 → 9 0.203 0.609 0.997 0.756 3.900 56
9 → 6 → 9 0.144 0.512 0.997 0.676 2.700 49
9 → 9 → 9  (no bottleneck) 0.043 0.525 0.997 0.688 3.100 77
9 → 12 → 6 → 12 → 9 0.061 0.459 0.986 0.627 7.900 103

Among designs that compress the input, 9 → 4 → 9 scored best (F1 0.76). The design without any bottleneck scored F1 0.69; with no compression the network can simply copy its input, so it is only a baseline. Deeper networks overfit the normal rows and raised more false alarms. The experiment used a 20,000-row sample for speed.

6. Anomaly scoring

For each row the model's reconstruction error is computed per feature, divided by that feature's normal error range, and the worst feature gives the row's anomaly score. This stops one large mistake from being averaged away by five normal features, and the worst feature also provides a plain-English reason. Severity is the score relative to the threshold (High ≥ 150×, Medium ≥ 20×).

7. Threshold analysis

Method threshold alerts precision recall f1
Percentile (99.6th of normal scores) 31.383 437 0.760 0.933 0.837
Mean + 3 standard deviations 360.309 158 0.880 0.390 0.541
Median + 3 × MAD (robust) 0.310 2815 0.126 0.997 0.224
Q3 + 3 × IQR (box-plot rule) 0.610 1215 0.292 0.997 0.452
Best F1 on training labels (reference only) 52.574 342 0.898 0.862 0.880

The live threshold uses the 99.6th percentile of scores on the cleaned training rows. Methods assuming a bell-shaped score (mean + 3σ) or using very tight robust spreads (MAD, IQR) were poorly matched to these heavy-tailed scores: they either missed many errors or raised thousands of alerts. A sensitivity control and an alternative-method selector let operators move along the curve.

8. Detection workflow and FastAPI service

The trained model is exposed through a FastAPI service (api.py) that validates input with Pydantic and returns the score, severity, reason, likely error type, estimated revenue at risk and suggested action. The same scoring code serves the dashboard.

Method Path Purpose
GET /health Service and model status
GET /model/info Model design and threshold
GET /thresholds All threshold methods and performance
GET /metrics Held-out evaluation
POST /score Score one record
POST /score/batch Score up to 5,000 records 
uvicorn api:app --reload      # then open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
python test_api.py            # automated API checks

Automated tests check health, normal records, a decimal-error record, a stale sync, input validation and batch scoring.

9. Evaluation

Evaluated on the held-out 30% of the data, which the model never saw during training.

Approach Alerts Precision Recall F1
Rules only (traditional monitoring) 223 92.8% 58.1% 71.5%
Autoencoder only 366 90.4% 93.0% 91.7%
Autoencoder + rules (hybrid) 366 90.4% 93.0% 91.7%

Rules only look at price gaps and sync age, so they cannot see stock problems. The autoencoder covers all six signals; the hybrid adds the rules as a safety net for obvious cases.

10. False-positive and error analysis

  • 35 false alarms, which is 0.18% of normal syncs.
  • The most common trigger was “Sync is late / stale” (46% of false alarms).
  • 3% of false alarms scored below twice the threshold, so they were borderline cases.
  • 25 real errors were missed; most were “stock_drift” (24).

False alarms and real errors have different signatures. A recurring pattern is the record right after a real error: when a price or stock count snaps back to normal it looks like a sudden change. The system therefore skips alerts triggered only by a sudden change in the sync right after an alert (recovery suppression):

Recovery suppression Alerts False alarms Precision Recall F1
Off (alert on every unusual sync) 437 105 76.0% 93.3% 83.7%
On (skip the sync right after an alert) 366 35 90.4% 93.0% 91.7%

10.1 Causes of false alarms

Cause False alarms
No known cause 19
Legitimate promotion (channel catching up) 16

Promotions create a short, legitimate disagreement: the master price drops first and each channel catches up an hour later. Bulk inventory deliveries move master and channel stock together, so they cancel out in the “change versus master” features and rarely cause alarms. Seasonal demand surges and unusual-but-valid channel activity are not simulated and are listed as limitations.

11. Limitations

Where the model may be unreliable, with the evidence from this project:

  • Insufficient history. With 1 day of training data F1 was 0.65; with 30 days it was 0.76 (table below).
  • New products and new sales channels. With no history there is no baseline price ratio and no normal pattern, so early scores are unreliable until enough syncs accumulate.
  • Promotional campaigns. A promotion makes channels briefly disagree with the master while they catch up; these appear as false alarms (section 10.1).
  • Bulk inventory updates. Handled well when master and channel move together, but a one-sided bulk change would look like stock drift.
  • Sudden demand changes. A genuine sales surge lowers stock cover quickly and can look like oversell risk. Not simulated here.
  • Synthetic data. Results show the method’s behaviour, not real-world performance. Mild errors overlap with normal noise.
  • Fixed threshold. Normal behaviour that drifts needs retraining. Single-record API calls cannot see sudden changes (no history).
  • Revenue at risk is an illustrative estimate based on stated assumptions.

12. Operational recommendations

  • Start with the Balanced alert level and review High alerts first; tune sensitivity using the false-alarm rate your team can handle.
  • Run batch scoring after each sync cycle or call the API from the integration job.
  • Record analyst decisions (the dashboard's status workflow) and use confirmed false positives to tune thresholds.
  • Retrain monthly or after major catalog, promotion or channel changes.
  • Keep the safety rules on for business-critical limits (very large price gaps, very old syncs).
  • Keep recovery suppression on so analysts are not alerted twice for one incident.
Error type Suggested response
Decimal / entry error Pause the listing on this channel and re-push the master price immediately.
Price mismatch Check the channel's price rules and the last price-feed job; re-sync the price.
Stale sync Check the integration job / API limits; trigger a manual sync.
Oversell risk Lower or zero the channel's available stock and re-sync inventory now.
Stock drift Reconcile channel stock against the ERP and fix the allocation rule.
Unusual pattern Review the SKU manually; compare recent syncs for this channel.

13. Conclusions and future work

An unsupervised autoencoder learned normal sync behavior without labels and, with a tuned threshold, found 93.0% of real errors at 90.4% precision on its own, and 93.0% recall when combined with simple rules. Future work: validate on real operational logs, add rolling-window and cross-channel features, per-product thresholds, sequence models, streaming ingestion and alert delivery to chat or email.
